entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
This covers a variety of citizenship topics. Students spend the first term reflecting on the value of thinking for the Christian life or on building helpful habits. The second term focuses on government as students explore the historical documents and decisions from this rotation. The year finishes with a term of economics where students learn a variety of economic theories.

This topic is included in the following course(s): Citizenship: Grade 10 (U.S.)

entries.title: Placement & Combining Tips

blocks.text: If you, the student, are learning at home, work to schedule a time with your teacher when you can complete the lessons from Ourselves or your Ethics reading together, as these lessons are much richer when shared and discussed.
Connect back to the previous lesson. (Optional for Current Events).
For news sources: Scan the headlines first to get an overview, and then choose a story to read.

Read the selection assigned or the news story chosen for the time assigned. For rich, dense, or more challenging books such as Ourselves, it is a good idea to read them aloud. Keep an eye out for quotes to put in your commonplace book or events or characters to put down in your Book of Centuries.

Process and integrate your reading by narrating either orally or in writing. Some lesson plans will give you a suggestion of how best to narrate. To keep yourself on track, you might want to set a timer so you stop reading with enough time to narrate.

After your narration, think about how what you read connects to other subjects, other books, other things you've read or watched, or seen in the past or present. For current events, look up where events occurred on a map and ask questions together to discern the quality of the piece. (e.g., Are there sources cited? Is there an obvious bias? If so, what do other authors have to say on this subject? Are arguments supported by evidence? Is that evidence credible?) Consider reading an alternative perspective.
Record important ideas in your Citizenship Notebooks. Make a calendar of current events.

These lessons are written directly to students, but to assist them throughout the year, please read through this section and the lesson plans so you are familiar with the instructions and flow of the lessons. You may also want to preview and choose which news sites to offer students.

Those educating at home might pick one lesson to read aloud (such as the Ethics readings on Cultural Engagement, Conscience, etc.) with their students to keep up the habit of oral narration and foster conversation and relationship and then simply give students these lesson plans and the rest of the books and check in with them throughout the term for conversation, support, and accountability. 

It is valuable for those in a classroom setting to also have a mix of lessons, which students complete themselves silently, and others read aloud and narrated together. Classroom settings lend themselves well to additional discussion and sharing at the end of lessons, after everyone has narrated either together or independently in writing.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Think: The Life of the Mind and the Love of God; Journal or Notebook; a Bible

➜ INTRO
The Gospel of Matthew records a conversation between Jesus and a lawyer. "Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?" Jesus replied, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment. And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets" (Matt. 22:36-40). This term, you will be challenged to cultivate the life of the mind in a way that results in obedience to the first and great commandment.

➜ READ
Introduction

➜ REFLECT/WRITE
Read and reflect on how Romans 11:36 and Colossians 1:15-17 relate to the reading in the book. Jot down your ideas or discuss with someone. 
---------------------------------------------------------------
⍞ Materials: Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones; a Journal or Notebook; a Bible

➜ INTRO
Habits play a significant role in Charlotte Mason's philosophy of education. According to Mason, "Now, habits which are allowed to fall into disuse are all the same as though they had never been formed; powers not exercised grow feeble and are lost. The ground which has been gained in half-a-dozen years may be lost in a single one" (Mason, Vol. 5, p.251). Mason reminds us that it is not only important to cultivate good habits, but it is equally imperative to exercise those habits, or else they will be lost.

This term, you will be led through several exercises to teach you how to identify and implement habits that result in life transformation. Some of these exercises include how to maintain the practice of habit-keeping so you do not lose momentum. You will refer to your journal or notebook several times during the term to complete the assigned exercises. 

➜ READ
Introduction - Ch.1

➜ NARRATE
Take a moment to narrate silently or aloud the main ideas of the reading. 

➜ REFLECT & WRITE
Looking back at the chapter as needed, in your journal, contrast goals and systems. Reflect on your life practices to see if you can identify systems that are at work in your life currently. Jot those down.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 13
lessons.body:
A Young Nation: American Government from 1800 to 1900
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
Welcome back to American Government! Last year, you learned about the formation of the American Government and the reasoning behind why the Constitution and Bill of Rights were drafted and negotiated as they were. This year, we move forward to the period from 1800 to 1900 and study the way in which the new government began to take action and shape the first hundred years of our country’s history. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 1 
With any time that you have remaining, read your summary statements and skim any written narrations from the last two years of American Government. Your summary statements should cover the time periods from Rotation 1 (800 CE - 1650 CE) and Rotation 2 (1650 CE - 1800 CE). 

➜ REFLECT & DISCUSS
Talk about the summary statements you have reviewed with your teacher or classmates. What did you remember? What had you forgotten? Did anything come to mind as you were reviewing that you had not thought about before?
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
One week is built in at the end of this term for “catch-up” reading, in case you miss a week or a reading takes you longer than your allotted time to complete. Please do not skip ahead if you have not completed the lesson from the week before – work through the weeks chronologically and use the catch-up week (Week 11) as necessary.  

• EXTRA HELPING
Guide students in creating a bulleted list of keywords that they noticed while reading their summary statements or during their discussion. Keywords can be words that were repeated frequently, or that stood out to the student for any particular reason (there is no “right” set of keywords). This activity is optional because it requires students to exercise a higher-level analysis and might not be a useful reflective tool for all students.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 14
lessons.body:
Western Expansion and the Missouri Compromise (1820)
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
The United States nearly doubled in size following the purchase of the Louisiana Territory from France. As new states began to petition Congress for entry to the country, the issue of slavery began to divide the nation. In 1820, Congress passed the Missouri Compromise, defining geographical boundaries that would determine whether slavery would be legal in new states. The Compromise would be followed by a series of legislative acts that together attempted to bind the new country together in the face of rapid land expansion and deep divides over slavery. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 2

➜ WRITE
Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 15
lessons.body:
Western Expansion and the Compromise of 1850
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
Although the Missouri Compromise remained in effect, the acquisition of the western territory from Texas to modern-day California following the Mexican-American War reignited the question of whether new states formed from this territory would be admitted as slave states or free states. To maintain a tentative balance of slave to free states across the nation, Congress passed the Compromise of 1850 after efforts to ban slavery entirely from the new territory failed. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 3

➜ WRITE
Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 16
lessons.body:
Western Expansion and the Kansas-Nebraska Act
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed the Missouri Compromise in its entirety and allowed the new territories of Kansas and Nebraska to decide the question of whether slavery would be allowed in the territories by popular sovereignty – by a vote of the people of the territories. Violence stemming from pro-slavery and abolitionist clashes in Kansas and in Washington, D.C., earned the nickname “Bleeding Kansas” and foreshadowed the start of the Civil War. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 4

➜ WRITE
Consider the three major pieces of Congressional legislation that you have studied over the last three weeks: the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act.  Write a summary statement or short narration explaining your thoughts in response to these questions.
• Why do you think that Representatives and Senators in Congress increasingly decided to turn the slavery question over to popular vote? 
• What benefits are there to a popular vote? 
•What drawbacks or dangers might there be to a popular vote?

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 17
lessons.body:
Treaties and the Removal of Tribal Nations (Part I)
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
Treaties are a tool that the Constitution allows the President to use in order to make formal agreements between the United States and another nation. Over the first four decades of the 19th century, the United States began to engage in treaty-making with American Indian Tribes, located in what are now the southern states of Tennessee, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, and Mississippi, with the goal of removing these Tribes from the south and relocating them west of the Mississippi River. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 5

➜ WRITE
Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 18
lessons.body:
Treaties and the Removal of Tribal Nations (Part II)
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 1

➜ INTRO
With the Indian Removal Act of 1830, Congress indicated its support for the removal of tribes, specifically authorizing then-President Andrew Jackson to use treaties to effect land exchanges, trading land west of the Mississippi to tribes in exchange for tribal land in the south. But was the Indian Removal Act constitutional, and were the treaties themselves enforceable? We will explore the Act and its impact further in this week’s reading.  

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 1
Week 6

➜ WRITE
Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 19
lessons.body:
Tribal Nations before the Supreme Court
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 2

➜ INTRO
While President Jackson and Congress worked to remove Tribes from the South by means of treaties and federal legislation, the Cherokee Nation sought to enforce its treaty rights before the Supreme Court. Over the course of two decisions within the span of the same number of years, the Supreme Court set precedent that would define the rights and status of Tribes into the modern day, and by extension, undermined the integrity of the federal government’s treaty-making with these Tribes. The Indian Appropriations Act, passed in 1871 by Congress, would end treaty-making with Tribes altogether. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 2
Week 7

➜ WRITE 
Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 20
lessons.body:
Congress & Southern Secession
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 2

➜ INTRO
On December 20, 1860, South Carolina seceded from the United States. Over the next seven months, ten more states would follow suit. Four of these states drafted formal Declarations of Causes that set forth their justifications for secession. This week, we will explore these Declarations in more detail and consider the impact that southern secession had on the federal Congress and the states left behind.

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 2
Week 8

➜ WRITE
Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.  Consider how the various southern secession documents compare or contrast with the Declaration of Independence. What strikes you as similar or different? Among other things, you want to think about the organization or length of the documents, the reasons given for separation, and the historical events ongoing at the time that each document was signed.
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
If you have a group of students, pose this question for group discussion as an alternative to traditional narration. If you are the only student in your class, jot down some of the similarities or differences that you think of.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 21
lessons.body:
Congress & the Reconstruction Acts
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 2

➜ INTRO
Following the end of the Civil War and preliminary reconstruction efforts by President Johnson, Congress exerted control over the Reconstruction project by passing a series of acts now known as the Reconstruction Acts. These Acts, passed over a presidential veto by Johnson, established military control in southern states that had seceded and established strict standards for readmission to the Union. 

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Part 2
Week 9

➜ WRITE
Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

lessons.title: 40m Econ/Civics: Grade 10 (U.S.) - Lesson 22
lessons.body:
“Defective from the Start”: The Constitution, Slavery, & the Civil War Amendments
⍞ Materials: Reading PDF Part 2

➜ INTRO
In addition to taking control of Reconstruction following the close of the Civil War, Congress also proposed three amendments to the Constitution. These amendments, now known as the Civil War Amendments, banned slavery and established a series of protections and rights that are now foundational to how we think about citizenship in the United States. It would be five years before these amendments were fully ratified by the states, and it would be nearly a hundred more years until the Civil Rights Movement would take up the vision for justice and equality that these amendments had begun to advance.

➜ READ
∞ Link: Reading PDF Parţ 2
Week 10

➜ WRITE
Write a summary statement or short narration describing the main ideas from this week’s reading.

Exam Week

➜ EXAMS
Answer question(s) related to the course.

Questions will come from:
What Would Keynes Do?

terms.content:
· Think: The Life of the Mind and the Love of God: Choose one question to answer:
Write about four things you learned from the book.
or
Explain why anti-intellectualism is not compatible with Christianity.

· Atomic Habits: Define the Four Laws of Behavior Change presented in the book.

· Reading PDF: Tell about the expansion of the United States into the southeast and the relocation of Tribal Nations. What actions did Congress, the President, and/or the Supreme Court take with regard to Removal? How did tribes respond to Removal efforts? 
                                                 OR 
Tell about the Southern secession and the actions that Congress took in response to the outbreak of the Civil War and as part of Reconstruction following the Civil War. Bonus: How many branches of government became involved in the reconstruction work, and what role did those branches play?

· What Would Keynes Do?: Choose one question or quote and explain in light of the economic principles you have learned, giving examples from everyday life around you: 
- Explain rational choice theory and its impact on decision-making in a person's life. 
- In What Would Keynes Do?, the author quotes Steven Levitt, "Economists love incentives. The typical economist believes the world has not yet invented a problem that he cannot fix if given a free hand to design the proper incentive schemes." 
- How do we best manage common resources? 
- "We give to charity in order to better provide public goods not supplied by the market."
